set1.q: Which disorder results from an organic rather than an inorganic occupational or environmental exposure?
opts: Coal workers' pneumoconiosis is on the inorganic side of the exposure list: coal dust is an inorganic dust taken up by alveolar macrophages to form coal macules. Tell: pneumoconiosis means inorganic or silicate dust, while organic dusts cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

Silicosis comes from free crystalline silica dust in mining, sandblasting, quarry work and stone work, an inorganic exposure on the same list as asbestosis. Tell: mineral dust is inorganic; bird, hay and mold sources are organic.

Asbestosis follows inhaled asbestos fibers from insulation, demolition, shipyards and construction, and it sits on the inorganic exposure list. Tell: fibers and mineral dusts are inorganic, while animal and plant material such as feathers and moldy hay is organic.

Correct. The organic exposures that cause interstitial lung disease include bird fancier's lung, farmer's lung, mushroom worker's lung and hot tub lung. Inhaled organic dusts such as bird excreta and feathers cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

set1.q: Besides a current chest radiograph, which screening test should a patient with silicosis have?
opts: A yearly ophthalmologic evaluation belongs to sarcoidosis follow-up, to identify and manage ocular inflammation. Tell: eye monitoring is for sarcoidosis, while silica's added risk is tuberculosis, screened with a skin test.

Pleural fluid cytology diagnoses mesothelioma, the pleural cancer of asbestos exposure; it is not screening for silicosis. Tell: asbestos threatens the pleura, while silica raises tuberculosis risk and calls for a tuberculin skin test.

Antibodies to the agent in serum give the definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis from organic dust; they are not a screening test in silicosis. Tell: silicosis screening targets tuberculosis, its added infection risk.

Correct. Silicosis increases the risk of tuberculosis, so patients should have a tuberculin skin test and a current chest radiograph. Treatment is otherwise largely supportive: oxygen, physiotherapy, medications, vaccinations and smoking cessation.

set1.q: Pneumoconiosis is a chronic fibrotic lung disease caused by inhaling which material?
opts: Inhaled chlorine, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, ammonia or smoke cause acute injury, a direct pulmonary cause of acute respiratory distress syndrome, not a chronic fibrotic pneumoconiosis. Tell: a toxic gas injures quickly, while dust disease is chronic.

Amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutic agents are treatment-related causes of interstitial lung disease and drug-induced pulmonary toxicity, not a pneumoconiosis. Tell: the word pneumoconiosis means lung disease from inhaled inorganic dust.

Correct. Pneumoconiosis is a chronic fibrotic lung disease caused by the inhalation of coal dust or various inorganic or silicate dusts. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis, asbestosis and silicosis all come from these inorganic exposures.
Organic dusts such as moldy hay

Organic dusts such as moldy hay, bird excreta and feathers cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis, an inflammatory disease from inhaled organic material. Tell: organic dust means hypersensitivity, while inorganic or silicate dust means pneumoconiosis.

set1.q: Which part of the lung does interstitial lung disease involve?
opts: The pleural lining is where mesothelioma, a cancer of that lining, and the pleural plaques of asbestos exposure arise; it is not the defining site of interstitial disease. Interstitial lung disease sits in the alveoli, alveolar ducts and respiratory bronchioles. Tell: interstitial means the gas-transfer tissue.

The larger airways are not the defined site: interstitial lung disease involves the portion of the lung that transfers gas, from the respiratory bronchioles out to the alveoli. Tell: the disease thickens the alveolar septa, so it sits where gas is exchanged, not where air is conducted.

The pulmonary vessels are not the site that defines this group; interstitial lung disease scars and inflames the alveoli, alveolar ducts and respiratory bronchioles. Tell: look for alveolar septal thickening and collagen deposition, which are changes in the gas-exchanging parenchyma.

Correct. Interstitial lung disease involves the parenchyma, the portion of the lung involved in gas transfer: the alveoli, alveolar ducts and respiratory bronchioles. It is characterized by alveolar septal thickening, fibroblast proliferation, collagen deposition and, if prolonged, pulmonary fibrosis.

set1.q: In which decades of life does sarcoidosis usually begin?
opts: Sarcoidosis is a disease of adults, with onset in the third and fourth decades of life, not of childhood and adolescence. Tell: the onset window is young to middle adulthood, so a first presentation in the first two decades does not fit the usual pattern.

Correct. Sarcoidosis has its onset in the third and fourth decades of life. It more frequently affects women and has a higher occurrence in North American Black and Northern European white populations; its etiology is unknown.

The fifth and sixth decades are later than the usual onset; sarcoidosis typically begins in the third and fourth decades of life. Tell: sarcoidosis is a younger adult's disease, while the older-adult rule in this topic belongs to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Age over 65 is the threshold for diagnosing idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis without biopsy, not the onset of sarcoidosis, which begins in the third and fourth decades. Tell: older age points toward pulmonary fibrosis; young adulthood points toward sarcoidosis.

set1.q: Which is the most common subtype of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia?
opts: Correct. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common subtype of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, which is itself the most common diagnosis among patients with interstitial lung disease. Treatment plan and prognosis depend on the subtype diagnosed.

Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia is one of the histopathologic patterns, notable because corticosteroids may be used for it, but it is not the most common subtype. Tell: the dominant subtype is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, the one that needs no further label.

Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia is a subtype in which corticosteroids may be used, but it is not the most common one. Tell: the steroid-responsive subtypes are a short, rarer list; the most common subtype is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Acute interstitial pneumonia is one of the listed histopathologic patterns, not the most common. Tell: the subtype that dominates idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, and that has its own no-biopsy criteria in older adults, is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

set1.q: Which laboratory result is elevated in 40 to 80% of patients with sarcoidosis?
opts: A high antinuclear antibody level points to the collagen vascular diseases, the autoimmune connective tissue group, not to sarcoidosis. Tell: sarcoidosis raises the angiotensin-converting enzyme and the sedimentation rate, not autoimmune antibodies.

A positive cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a granulomatous vasculitis rather than sarcoidosis. Tell: both form granulomas, but the antibody clue belongs to the vasculitis; the enzyme clue belongs to sarcoidosis.

Antiglomerular and antipulmonary alveolar basement membrane antibodies identify Goodpasture syndrome, glomerulonephritis with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage. Tell: basement membrane antibodies mean kidney and lung bleeding, not sarcoidosis.

Correct. Angiotensin-converting enzyme levels are elevated in 40 to 80% of patients with sarcoidosis. Other laboratory findings include leukopenia, eosinophilia, an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hypercalcemia in about 5% of patients and hypercalciuria.

set1.q: Which occupation exposes workers to free crystalline silica dust?
opts: Bird excreta and feathers are organic dusts that cause hypersensitivity pneumonitis, bird fancier's lung, not silicosis. Tell: animal and plant material is organic and drives hypersensitivity, while crystalline silica comes from sand and stone work.

Cheese maker's lung is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis from handling moldy organic products, with symptoms hours after exposure. Tell: moldy organic material means hypersensitivity, while silica dust comes from mining, sandblasting, quarry and stone work.

Correct. Silicosis follows exposure to free crystalline silica dust (silicon dioxide) in mining, sandblasting, quarry work and stone work. The silica deposits in the alveoli, where macrophage invasion causes chronic inflammation, fibrosis and nodular lesions.

Demolition is an asbestos exposure, listed with insulation, shipyard and construction work, leading to asbestosis with pleural plaques and ferruginous bodies. Tell: tearing down buildings means asbestos; sand and stone mean silica.

set1.q: When may lung transplant be indicated in coal workers' pneumoconiosis?
opts: Pleural plaques are the most common chest radiograph finding of asbestos exposure, not a coal workers' pneumoconiosis milestone, and they are not a transplant trigger. Tell: in coal workers, transplant is considered for severe disease.

Correct. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis has no effective curative treatment, so care is supportive with oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, and lung transplant may be indicated in severe cases. Complicated disease can progress to progressive massive fibrosis.

Simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis is usually asymptomatic, with pulmonary function tests that can be unimpressive, so it does not call for transplant. Tell: transplant is kept for severe disease, not for coal macules without symptoms.

Diagnosis starts supportive care, oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, rather than transplant. Tell: transplant enters the plan when the disease becomes severe, not when it is first found on a chest radiograph.

set1.q: What is the outlook for a patient with mesothelioma?
opts: Correct. Mesothelioma is incurable with poor long-term survival; no treatment is known to prolong survival, and care is primarily supportive. It is nearly always caused by asbestos exposure, and the diagnosis can come from pleural fluid cytology.
No treatment is known to prolong survival in mesothelioma, so early surgery is not described as curative; care is primarily supportive. Tell: the pleural cancer of asbestos exposure is incurable.

Recovery of pulmonary function over 6 to 12 months describes survivors of acute respiratory distress syndrome, not mesothelioma, which is incurable. Tell: a year-long recovery belongs to an acute injury, while mesothelioma has poor long-term survival.

Control with corticosteroids describes about 90% of sarcoidosis cases, not a pleural cancer; mesothelioma care is primarily supportive. Tell: steroid-responsive granulomas are sarcoidosis, while mesothelioma is an incurable asbestos cancer.

set1.q: Which statement fits the definition of interstitial lung disease?
opts: A cancer of the lung tissue

Interstitial lung disease is not malignant; the cancers in this topic, mesothelioma and lung carcinoma, are complications of asbestos exposure rather than the disease itself. Tell: interstitial disease scars and inflames the parenchyma without being a cancer.

Correct. Interstitial lung disease is a broad category of more than 200 disorders characterized by scarring (fibrosis) and/or inflammation of the lung parenchyma. By definition it is not malignant and not caused by an infectious etiology.
A single disorder with one cause

Interstitial lung disease is not one disorder: it is a broad category of more than 200 disorders that are difficult to classify, with known and unknown causes. Tell: the category is defined by scarring and inflammation of the parenchyma, not by a single cause.

Infection is excluded by the definition: interstitial lung disease is not caused by an infectious etiology, even though it involves the alveoli. Tell: inflammation and scarring without infection or cancer is what defines the group.

set1.q: About how long after asbestos exposure do patients with asbestosis usually seek medical attention?
opts: A single year is far too short for asbestosis; patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after exposure, which is why the occupational history must reach back many years. Tell: asbestos disease is measured in years to decades, not months.

Five years is shorter than the usual interval: patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after exposure, within the 10 to 20 year span of the asbestos history. Tell: the presenting interval is about 15 years.

Correct. The asbestos history spans 10 to 20 years, and patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after exposure. Imaging is often normal early in the disease, so the long gap and the occupational history point to the diagnosis.

Thirty years overshoots the usual interval; patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after asbestos exposure. Tell: think 15 years, the middle of the 10 to 20 year span in the asbestos history.

set1.q: Into which two groups are interstitial lung diseases divided by their tissue response?
opts: Interstitial lung disease is by definition not malignant and not caused by an infectious etiology, so these cannot be its two groups. The groups are inflammation with fibrosis and granulomatous reactions. Tell: cancer and infection sit outside the definition itself.

Acute and chronic are stages that most interstitial lung diseases pass through within either group, not the two groups themselves. The groups are inflammation with fibrosis and granulomatous reactions. Tell: a stage describes timing, while a group describes the tissue response.

Correct. Interstitial lung diseases fall into two groups by tissue response: inflammation with fibrosis, or granulomatous reactions. Each group can be further divided into known and unknown causes, and most of these diseases have acute and chronic stages.

Obstructive and restrictive are pulmonary function patterns, not tissue responses, and interstitial lung disease produces the restrictive one, with reduced lung volumes. Tell: the two groups describe what the tissue does, scar or form granulomas, not what spirometry shows.

set1.q: Below what ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen is the oxygenation criterion for acute respiratory distress syndrome met?
opts: Under 100 mm Hg marks severe disease, not the entry threshold; ratios between 100 and 300 already meet the oxygenation criterion as mild or moderate disease. Tell: 100 is the severe cutoff, while 300 is the diagnostic one.

Two hundred is the boundary between mild (200 to 300 mm Hg) and moderate (100 to 200 mm Hg) disease, so a ratio of 250 already meets the criterion. Tell: 200 splits mild from moderate; the diagnostic threshold is 300.

Correct. The oxygenation impairment threshold is a ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen under 300 mm Hg (or a ratio of arterial oxygen saturation to fraction of inspired oxygen under 315). Within it, 200 to 300 is mild, 100 to 200 moderate and under 100 severe.

The threshold is under 300 mm Hg, so a ratio between 300 and 400 falls outside the oxygenation criterion. Tell: the mild class tops out at 300 mm Hg, and nothing above it counts as acute respiratory distress syndrome.

set1.q: Which computed tomography finding characterizes idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia?
opts: Correct. Computed tomography in idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia shows diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing, while the chest radiograph shows progressive fibrosis over several areas. On high-resolution scanning in a patient over 65, it is one of the four no-biopsy criteria.

Eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes is the silicosis finding, alongside nodular opacities of 1 to 10 mm. Tell: calcified hilar node rims point to silica; pleural-based honeycombing points to pulmonary fibrosis.

Pleural plaques are the most common radiographic finding in asbestosis, with linear streaking at the bases, and computed tomography is the preferred imaging there. Tell: plaques on the pleura mean asbestos, while honeycombing beneath the pleura means fibrosis.

Upper-lung nodular opacities fit the dust diseases: coal macules of 2 to 5 mm in the upper lung fields and silicotic nodules carried to the upper lobes as a lighter dust. Tell: nodules up top mean inhaled mineral dust; patchy honeycombing means idiopathic fibrosis.

set1.q: Amiodarone, nitrofurantoin, methotrexate and radiation fall under which class of interstitial lung disease?
opts: Granulomatous lung disease, sarcoidosis and hypersensitivity pneumonitis, is its own box in the classification, not where medications are filed. Drugs and radiation are a known, treatment-related cause. Tell: granulomatous describes the tissue response, not a drug exposure.

Correct. In the classification of interstitial lung disease, the exposure branch of known causes holds a treatment-related box listing radiation, methotrexate, amiodarone, nitrofurantoin and chemotherapeutics. Chemotherapeutic agents, amiodarone and nitrofurantoin also cause drug-induced pulmonary toxicity.

The occupational box under known causes holds work exposures such as asbestosis and silicosis, which come from inhaled dusts. Drugs and radiation sit in the neighboring treatment-related box. Tell: a medication or therapy points to treatment related; a job points to occupational.

Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, form the unknown-cause branch, where no exposure is found. A named drug or radiation is a known cause. Tell: if you can name the agent, the cause is known.

set1.q: Which occupation carries a risk of asbestos exposure?
opts: Quarry work is a silica exposure, listed with mining, sandblasting and stone work as a cause of silicosis with upper-lobe nodules and eggshell hilar calcification. Tell: stone and sand jobs point to silica; asbestos comes from insulation and shipyards.

Cheese maker's lung is a hypersensitivity pneumonitis from inhaled organic material, with fever and cough hours after exposure, not an asbestos exposure. Tell: moldy organic products point to hypersensitivity; insulation and shipyards point to asbestos.

Correct. Asbestos fiber exposure comes from insulation, demolition, shipyard and construction work, with a history spanning 10 to 20 years, and patients usually seek medical attention about 15 years after exposure. The work history is the key clue.

Sandblasting exposes workers to free crystalline silica dust, along with mining, quarry work and stone work, and leads to silicosis. Tell: sand and stone mean silica, while insulation, demolition, ships and construction mean asbestos.

set1.q: Which interstitial lung disease can produce an episodic presentation?
opts: Correct. An episodic presentation is less common in interstitial lung disease and can be seen with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, where inhaled organic material leads to illness after exposure, and symptoms can be reversible if the problem is caught early.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a chronic presentation, progressing over months to years, not one that comes and goes. Tell: an insidious dry cough with steady exertional dyspnea means chronic fibrosis; episodes mean an exposure-driven disease.

Pneumoconiosis presents chronically, over months to years, from long-term inhalation of inorganic dust, and simple disease is usually asymptomatic. Tell: inorganic dust disease is chronic; episodes after exposure suggest an organic antigen.

Drug-induced interstitial lung disease is named with sarcoidosis as most common among subacute presentations, over weeks to months, not episodic ones. Tell: subacute means drugs and sarcoidosis; episodic means hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

set1.q: In the laboratory workup of interstitial lung disease, what does an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate point to?
opts: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is paired with a positive c-ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody), not with the sedimentation rate. Tell: the cytoplasmic antineutrophil antibody is the polyangiitis clue; the sedimentation rate is the sarcoidosis clue.

Correct. Among the laboratory clues in interstitial lung disease, an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate points to active sarcoidosis, which can also show eosinophilia and, in some patients, an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level and hypercalcemia.

Collagen vascular disease is suggested by a high antinuclear antibody level, the autoimmune marker in the workup, rather than by the sedimentation rate. Tell: antinuclear antibody for collagen vascular disease; sedimentation rate for active sarcoidosis.

Goodpasture syndrome is identified by antiglomerular and antipulmonary alveolar basement membrane antibodies, with glomerulonephritis and diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage. Tell: basement membrane antibodies mean Goodpasture; a raised sedimentation rate means active sarcoidosis.

set1.q: Which evaluation belongs to the yearly follow-up of patients with sarcoidosis?
opts: A tuberculin skin test with a current chest radiograph is the screening owed to patients with silicosis because of their increased risk of tuberculosis. Tell: silica raises tuberculosis risk, while sarcoidosis follow-up looks for eye, heart and lung involvement.

Pleural fluid cytology diagnoses mesothelioma, the pleural cancer of asbestos exposure that often develops effusions. It has no place in routine sarcoidosis follow-up. Tell: sarcoidosis needs a yearly eye examination, electrocardiogram and lung testing.

Antibodies to the inhaled agent give the definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis; sarcoidosis has no exposure antigen to measure. Tell: sarcoidosis follow-up is a yearly examination, function tests, radiograph, electrocardiogram, chemistry panel and eye evaluation.

Correct. Patients with sarcoidosis require a yearly physical examination, pulmonary function tests, chest radiograph, electrocardiogram, chemistry panel and an ophthalmologic evaluation to identify and manage ocular inflammation. Iritis and uveitis are indications for corticosteroids.

set1.q: Which cause of acute respiratory distress syndrome is a direct pulmonary insult?
opts: Sepsis is the leading systemic trigger, with about one third of cases initially presenting with sepsis syndrome, but it injures the lung indirectly. Tell: sepsis is systemic; aspiration damages the parenchyma directly.

Severe pancreatitis is a major systemic insult, listed with sepsis, shock and nonthoracic trauma, not a direct lung injury. Tell: an abdominal source acts through the bloodstream; aspiration acts on the lung itself.

Multiple blood transfusions are an iatrogenic systemic risk, listed with disseminated intravascular coagulation and cardiopulmonary bypass. Tell: transfusion injures the lung through the circulation; aspiration of gastric contents is a direct insult.

Correct. Direct pulmonary causes include aspiration of gastric contents, diffuse pneumonia, lung contusion, toxic gas inhalation, near-drowning, and fat, air, amniotic fluid or thrombus emboli. Sepsis, pancreatitis, shock, trauma outside the chest and blood transfusions are systemic causes.

opts: The history comes first: identifying the agent responsible is the first treatment step, and the exposure history is how it is found. Tell: find and remove the antigen, then add corticosteroids if the case is severe.

Correct. In hypersensitivity pneumonitis, corticosteroids may be helpful in severe cases, along with other immunosuppressant medications, after the responsible agent has been identified and is being avoided. Supportive treatment includes oxygen, bronchodilators and pain medications.

Mild acute disease is handled by identifying and avoiding the agent; corticosteroids are described for severe cases. Tell: symptoms can be reversible when caught early and the exposure stops, so steroids are kept for severe disease.
In place of avoiding the agent

Avoiding the agent is the core of treatment, because continued exposure may lead to a worsened disease state; steroids add to avoidance in severe cases rather than replacing it. Tell: avoidance always comes first.

opts: Correct. The pulmonary hemorrhage syndromes, or alveolar filling disorders, with an inflammatory and fibrotic response, are Goodpasture syndrome, idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis and isolated pulmonary capillaritis. Goodpasture syndrome is marked by basement membrane antibodies.

Systemic sclerosis is a connective tissue disease (think autoimmune) with an inflammatory and fibrotic lung response, listed with lupus and rheumatoid arthritis rather than with the hemorrhage syndromes. Tell: bleeding into the alveoli defines the hemorrhage group.

Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease with noncaseating granulomas, not a pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome. Tell: the hemorrhage group fills the alveoli with blood; sarcoidosis forms granulomas in the lungs and lymph nodes.

Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common subtype of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, a scarring disease with pleural-based honeycombing, not a pulmonary hemorrhage syndrome. Tell: fibrosis scars the interstitium; the hemorrhage group fills the alveoli with blood.

opts: Correct. Among the laboratory findings in interstitial lung disease, a high antinuclear antibody level points to the collagen vascular diseases, the autoimmune connective tissue group that includes lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and systemic sclerosis.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is suggested by a positive c-ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody), not by the antinuclear antibody. Tell: antinuclear antibody for collagen vascular disease, cytoplasmic antineutrophil antibody for polyangiitis.

Active sarcoidosis is suggested by an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and sarcoidosis can also show eosinophilia, hypercalcemia and an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme. Tell: a high antinuclear antibody points to autoimmune collagen vascular disease instead.

Eosinophilic pneumonia, like sarcoidosis and drug-induced disease, is suggested by eosinophilia, not by antinuclear antibodies. Tell: eosinophils point to eosinophilic, drug-induced or sarcoid disease; antinuclear antibodies point to collagen vascular disease.

opts: Stage I is bilateral hilar adenopathy alone, without parenchymal involvement, and it carries the best prognosis. Tell: once the parenchyma is involved alongside the enlarged hilar nodes, the stage has moved up to II.

Correct. Stage II sarcoidosis shows hilar adenopathy with parenchymal involvement. Stage I is bilateral hilar adenopathy alone, stage III is parenchymal involvement alone with diffuse reticular infiltrates, and stage IV is advanced fibrosis with honeycombing.
Stage III is parenchymal involvement alone, diffuse reticular infiltrates without the hilar adenopathy. Tell: nodes plus parenchyma is stage II, while parenchyma without the nodes is stage III.

Stage IV is advanced fibrosis with evidence of honeycombing, hilar retraction, bullae, cysts and emphysema, beyond simple parenchymal involvement. Tell: honeycombing and bullae mean stage IV; adenopathy with infiltrates means stage II.

set1.q: Which core diagnostic criterion separates acute respiratory distress syndrome from cardiogenic pulmonary edema?
opts: The imaging criterion requires new bilateral opacities that are not explained by effusion, atelectasis or nodules, so opacities explained by effusion argue against the diagnosis. Tell: the opacities must be unexplained by those causes.

The onset criterion is within 7 days of a known clinical insult; weeks to months is the subacute presentation of interstitial lung disease. Tell: distress syndrome is acute, with dyspnea 12 to 48 hours after the insult.

The imaging criterion is bilateral pulmonary opacities, and the infiltrates rapidly progress to confluent opacities. Tell: one-sided opacities do not meet the criterion; the process involves both lungs.
Not fully explained by heart failure

Correct. A core criterion is noncardiogenic origin: respiratory failure not fully explained by heart failure or fluid overload. Cardiogenic pulmonary edema, the main differential, shows cardiomegaly, vascular engorgement and batwing perihilar opacities, and echocardiography helps exclude it.

set1.q: What is the most common presenting symptom of interstitial lung disease?
opts: Correct. Fibrosis makes the lung tissue stiff and restrictive, no longer expanding as it once did, which makes breathing harder; patients most commonly present with shortness of breath, typically progressive exertional dyspnea, sometimes with a persistent nonproductive cough.

The cough of interstitial lung disease is persistent and nonproductive, not productive, and even so it is less common than breathlessness as the presenting complaint. Tell: a dry cough fits scarred, stiff lung tissue; dyspnea is the most common presentation.

Hemoptysis is on the list of presenting symptoms but is not the common one; stiff, restrictive lungs make shortness of breath the usual complaint. Tell: hemoptysis is a listed but less usual symptom, while progressive exertional dyspnea leads.

Chest pain can occur in interstitial lung disease but is a less usual complaint than dyspnea. Lung that cannot expand is what makes breathing hard. Tell: the leading complaint follows from the restrictive physiology, which is breathlessness, first on exertion and later at rest.

opts: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is not routine; it is reserved for severe, refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: the first step is to identify and treat the underlying insult promptly.

Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe disease and is not replaced by extracorporeal support, which is a salvage option for severe, refractory cases. Tell: proning comes earlier; extracorporeal support comes last.

Correct. Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is a salvage option reserved for severe, refractory acute respiratory distress syndrome, after the precipitant is treated and low tidal volume ventilation and early proning in moderate to severe disease have been used.

Mild disease, a ratio of 200 to 300 mm Hg, is managed with treatment of the precipitant, low tidal volumes and conservative fluids; extracorporeal support is reserved for severe, refractory cases. Tell: salvage means last resort.

opts: Waiting for a hemoglobin of 5 g/dL goes below the stated transfusion threshold of 7 g/dL. Tell: the threshold is restrictive, because higher targets do not improve outcomes, but it is set at 7 g/dL, not lower.

Correct. Patients with acute respiratory distress syndrome are transfused at a hemoglobin of 7 g/dL; higher hemoglobin targets do not improve patient outcomes. Supranormal, inotrope-driven oxygen delivery is avoided because it can cause harm.
A threshold of 9 g/dL is a higher hemoglobin target, and higher targets do not improve patient outcomes in acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: transfuse at 7 g/dL; aiming higher adds nothing.

A target of 10 g/dL is a higher hemoglobin goal, which does not improve patient outcomes, and pushing oxygen delivery to supranormal levels can cause harm. Tell: the transfusion threshold is 7 g/dL, not a near-normal hemoglobin.

set1.q: In which patients can idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis be diagnosed with 90% confidence without surgical lung biopsy?
opts: The no-biopsy rule applies to patients over 65, not to younger adults, and a smoking history is not one of its four features; otherwise idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia may require biopsy. Tell: the rule is built for older adults with clinical, functional and imaging features.

Honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography is one feature, and the rule is limited to patients over 65. Outside it, idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia may require biopsy for diagnosis. Tell: the rule joins age over 65 with four features.

Correct. In patients over 65 years of age, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis can be diagnosed with 90% confidence when there is idiopathic disease with inspiratory crackles, restrictive physiology, radiographic progressive fibrosis over several years, and diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography. Such patients do not need surgical lung biopsy.

Crackles are one of the four features, not enough by themselves; the over-65 rule also needs restrictive physiology, radiographic progressive fibrosis over several years and pleural-based honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography. Tell: age plus four features, not one.

opts: An elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is found in 40 to 80% of patients with sarcoidosis and plays no part in the pulmonary fibrosis criteria. Tell: this laboratory result supports sarcoidosis, while the fibrosis rule relies on examination, function testing and imaging.

Bilateral hilar adenopathy alone is the stage I chest radiograph of sarcoidosis, not a criterion for pulmonary fibrosis. The fibrosis criteria name progressive fibrosis on radiographs and pleural-based honeycombing on computed tomography. Tell: enlarged nodes mean sarcoidosis.

Correct. The four criteria are idiopathic disease with inspiratory crackles on examination, restrictive physiology on pulmonary function testing, radiographic evidence of progressive fibrosis over several years, and diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on high-resolution computed tomography.

The criteria require restrictive physiology, not obstruction: interstitial fibrosis lowers lung volumes with a normal to increased ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity. Tell: fibrosis restricts, so an obstructive result does not fit the rule.

opts: Hilar adenopathy alone is stage I, with the best prognosis, and it is not on the list of indications; pulmonary disease calls for corticosteroids when the lesions are progressive. Tell: treat progressive pulmonary lesions, not stable enlarged nodes.

Correct. Indications for oral corticosteroids in sarcoidosis include disabling constitutional symptoms, hypercalcemia, iritis, uveitis, arthritis, central nervous system or cardiac involvement, granulomatous hepatitis, cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum and progressive pulmonary lesions.

Erythema nodosum is the named exception: cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum are an indication, so this rash on the lower legs and ankles does not by itself call for oral corticosteroids. Tell: lupus pernio on the face counts; erythema nodosum does not.

An elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level is a diagnostic finding present in 40 to 80% of patients, not a listed indication for corticosteroids. Tell: steroids treat organ involvement such as hypercalcemia, eye or heart disease, not a laboratory value.

opts: Infliximab is the third immunosuppressant named for sarcoidosis that is refractory to or intolerant of corticosteroids, and it is not among the listed causes of interstitial lung disease. Tell: the drug that both treats sarcoidosis and causes lung disease is methotrexate.

Amiodarone is a treatment-related cause of interstitial lung disease and of drug-induced pulmonary toxicity, but it is not a treatment for sarcoidosis. Tell: amiodarone fits only the second half of the stem; methotrexate fits both halves.

Correct. Methotrexate is one of the immunosuppressants most commonly used when sarcoidosis is corticosteroid-intolerant or refractory, and it treats many autoimmune diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. It is also implicated as a cause of interstitial lung disease in the drug list and the treatment-related box.

Azathioprine is an immunosuppressant used for corticosteroid-intolerant or refractory sarcoidosis, but it does not appear on the list of drugs that cause interstitial lung disease. Tell: of the three sarcoidosis immunosuppressants, methotrexate is the one also listed as a cause.

set2.q: Which measure belongs to the supportive care of an adult with coal workers' pneumoconiosis?
opts: Correct. Supportive care for coal workers' pneumoconiosis includes oxygen, pneumococcal and influenza vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation, because no effective curative treatment is available. Lung transplant may be indicated in severe cases.
Lavage to remove the coal dust

No effective curative treatment is available, and lavage is a diagnostic study rather than a way to clear the dust. Tell: nothing clears or cures the disease, so care is oxygen, vaccinations, rehabilitation and smoking cessation.

Routine pulmonary artery catheters belong to acute respiratory distress syndrome care, where they are avoided because they offer no clinical benefit. Tell: a catheter is an intensive care device, not part of chronic dust-disease support.

Hemoglobin targets are a critical care question in acute respiratory distress syndrome, where transfusion at 7 g/dL is used because higher targets do not improve outcomes. Tell: chronic coal dust care is oxygen, vaccines, rehabilitation and cessation.

opts: The mortality benefit of early prone positioning is described for moderate to severe disease, not mild disease with a ratio of 200 to 300 mm Hg. Tell: proning is matched to the sicker classes, under 200 mm Hg.

Cardiomegaly with vascular engorgement points to cardiogenic pulmonary edema, the main differential, which a normal heart size argues against. Tell: proning is for moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, not for a cardiac cause of edema.
ruled out by a stated finding

Proning is an early measure; recovery is the later phase, when pulmonary function improves over 6 to 12 months and residual diffusion deficits are monitored. Tell: the word early matters, and the benefit is in moderate to severe disease.

Correct. Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, that is, a ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to inspired oxygen under 200 mm Hg. It is added to low tidal volume ventilation and treatment of the precipitant.

opts: Pleural plaques with linear streaking at the bases are the most common radiographic finding of asbestosis, not silicosis. Tell: plaques on the pleura point to asbestos, while calcified rims of the hilar nodes point to silica.

Diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing on computed tomography is the idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis picture. Tell: honeycombing beneath the pleura means idiopathic fibrosis; nodules with eggshell hilar calcification mean silica.

A normal heart size with air bronchograms in bilateral infiltrates is the imaging of acute respiratory distress syndrome, an acute illness rather than a dust disease. Tell: acute confluent infiltrates mean distress syndrome; eggshell nodes mean silica.

Correct. Silicosis imaging shows nodular opacities throughout, silicotic nodules of 1 to 10 mm forming nodular pulmonary fibrosis, and eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes.

set2.q: Over what period does pulmonary function generally recover after acute respiratory distress syndrome?
opts: One to 2 months is too short: lung function generally improves over 6 to 12 months after acute respiratory distress syndrome. Tell: recovery is year-long, so early follow-up should not expect normal function.

Correct. Pulmonary function improves over 6 to 12 months, generally recovering within about a year, though functional deficits often remain. Survivors need monitoring for residual diffusion deficits and treatment of post-intensive care muscle wasting, weakness and fatigue.
Recovery is described over 6 to 12 months, generally within about a year, not two years. Tell: the year-long recovery window ends around 12 months, even though some deficits persist.
Three to 4 years is far beyond the stated recovery period; lung function generally recovers over 6 to 12 months. Tell: think of about a year of recovery, with some residual diffusion deficits.

opts: Parotid gland enlargement is an examination finding of sarcoidosis, but it is not a skin lesion, so it cannot be the cutaneous exception the indications name. Tell: the exception is a rash, erythema nodosum, which appears with parotid enlargement on the examination list.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum are an indication for oral corticosteroids, so erythema nodosum, the itchy and painful rash on the lower legs and ankles, is the exception. Lupus pernio and other skin lesions still count toward treatment.

Lupus pernio, the skin sores on the face, is a cutaneous lesion other than erythema nodosum, so it is among the indications for oral corticosteroids. Tell: facial sores count toward steroids, while the leg and ankle rash is the exception.
Lesions on the back and arms

Skin lesions on the back, arms, neck, face and scalp are cutaneous lesions other than erythema nodosum and so fall within the corticosteroid indications. Tell: the one cutaneous exception is erythema nodosum on the lower legs and ankles.

opts: Early prone positioning decreases mortality in moderate to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, so it does offer benefit. Tell: proning helps the sicker classes, while the routine pulmonary artery catheter offers none.

Correct. Routine pulmonary artery catheters offer no clinical benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome and are avoided. Cardiac function is assessed instead with echocardiography to exclude hydrostatic cardiogenic pulmonary edema.

A conservative fluid protocol is recommended: restrictive fluids significantly increase ventilator-free days and shorten intensive care unit stays. Tell: restrictive fluids help, while the routine catheter adds nothing.
Low tidal volume ventilation is a core part of management, the strategy behind the 30% baseline mortality figure. Tell: low tidal volumes are recommended, while routine catheters are to be avoided.

opts: Permanent scar that stiffens the lung

Correct. Fibrosis is a response to an inflammatory source that lays down permanent scar tissue, making the lung tissue stiff and impairing gas exchange. The scarring damages the alveoli, most often permanently, and the stiff, restrictive lung causes shortness of breath.

Fibrosis is permanent scar tissue in the parenchyma, not a reversible airway swelling. The scar damages the alveoli, most often permanently. Tell: fibrosis means a fixed scar in the gas-exchanging tissue, so it does not simply resolve.

Fibrosis does the opposite: the tissue becomes stiff and restrictive and no longer expands as it once did, so lung volumes fall. Tell: scar makes the lung small and stiff, while an overinflated lung is the reverse picture.

Fibrosis is scar laid down in response to inflammation, not a malignant growth; interstitial lung disease is by definition not malignant. Tell: collagen from fibroblasts forms the scar, while a cancer would be a separate diagnosis.

opts: The chest radiograph is often normal in asbestosis, especially early, even though pleural plaques are its most common finding when present. Tell: when the plain film can miss early disease, the preferred study is computed tomography.

Echocardiography assesses cardiac function to exclude hydrostatic cardiogenic pulmonary edema in acute respiratory distress syndrome; it does not image asbestos-related lung or pleural disease. Tell: heart imaging excludes edema, while lung and pleural scarring needs computed tomography.

Pleural fluid cytology is how mesothelioma can be diagnosed when effusions develop; it examines fluid for cancer cells and is not an imaging study of asbestosis. Tell: cytology looks for the pleural cancer, while the preferred imaging is computed tomography.

Correct. Computed tomography is the preferred imaging for asbestosis. It can show pleural plaques, alveolitis and fibrosis, with honeycombing in advanced disease, while the plain chest radiograph is often normal, especially early in the disease.

Active sarcoidosis is suggested by an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and sarcoidosis can raise the angiotensin-converting enzyme level. Tell: sarcoidosis has its own laboratory markers, while the cytoplasmic antineutrophil antibody points to polyangiitis.

Correct. A positive c-ANCA (cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody) points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis, formerly Wegener's, a granulomatous vasculitis that is one of the interstitial lung diseases with a granulomatous response.

Goodpasture syndrome is identified by antiglomerular and antipulmonary alveolar basement membrane antibodies, and it combines glomerulonephritis with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage. Tell: basement membrane antibodies mean Goodpasture; the cytoplasmic antineutrophil antibody means polyangiitis.

set2.q: What size range do silicotic nodules span on imaging?
opts: Silicotic nodules are visible opacities of 1 to 10 mm, not specks under a millimeter. Tell: the silicotic range starts at 1 mm and runs to 10 mm, wider than the 2 to 5 mm coal macules.

Correct. Silicosis shows nodular opacities throughout the lungs, silicotic nodules of 1 to 10 mm, a nodular pulmonary fibrosis, together with eggshell calcification of the periphery of the hilar lymph nodes.

Two to 5 mm is the size of coal macules, the nodular opacities in the upper lung fields of coal workers' pneumoconiosis. Tell: coal macules are 2 to 5 mm; silicotic nodules span the wider 1 to 10 mm range.

Silicotic nodules top out at 10 mm; larger masses mean complicated disease, the conglomeration of the upper lungs. Tell: simple nodules are 1 to 10 mm, while conglomerate masses mark complicated silicosis.

set2.q: What is mesothelioma?
opts: A cancer of the pleural lining

Correct. Mesothelioma is primarily a pleural cancer, a cancer of the pleural lining, and is nearly always caused by asbestos exposure, whose fibers can penetrate further into the lung. Patients frequently develop pleural effusions.

Pleural plaques are the most common radiographic finding of asbestos exposure, not a cancer; mesothelioma is a pleural cancer that is incurable, with poor long-term survival. Tell: a plaque marks exposure, while mesothelioma is the malignancy.
A scar of the terminal bronchioles

Scarring of the terminal bronchioles, alveoli and interstitial spaces is asbestosis itself, fibrosis from chronic inflammation and macrophage invasion. Tell: asbestosis scars the lung tissue, while mesothelioma is cancer of the pleura.
An infection of the pleural space

Mesothelioma is a cancer, not an infection; it follows asbestos fibers that penetrate further into the lung and reach the pleural lining. Tell: asbestos exposure leads to scarring, plaques and cancer, not to infection.

set2.q: What share of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and familial lung fibrosis have a history of smoking?
opts: Twenty percent is the share of sarcoidosis patients with lung involvement who develop irreversible lung impairment, not the smoking rate in pulmonary fibrosis. Tell: the smoking history figure is a clear majority, two thirds to three quarters of patients.

Forty to 80% is the share of sarcoidosis patients with an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme level. The smoking history in pulmonary fibrosis is 67 to 75%. Tell: the wide 40 to 80 range belongs to a sarcoidosis laboratory test, not to a smoking history.

Correct. Between 67 and 75% of patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and familial lung fibrosis have a history of smoking. Smoking is the cause in the majority of cases of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, and cessation is critical to prolong life.

Ninety percent is the share of sarcoidosis cases responsive to corticosteroids and the confidence of diagnosing pulmonary fibrosis without biopsy in patients over 65. Tell: the smoking history figure is 67 to 75%, a majority but below 90.

set2.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis of sarcoidosis?
opts: The angiotensin-converting enzyme level is elevated in 40 to 80% of patients with sarcoidosis, so it supports the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. Tell: confirmation needs tissue that shows noncaseating granulomas.

The chest radiograph shows symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy and stages the disease from I to IV, but imaging does not confirm the diagnosis. Tell: staging describes extent, while a biopsy with noncaseating granulomas confirms.

Hypercalcemia occurs in about 5% of patients with sarcoidosis and is an indication for corticosteroids, but it is too uncommon and too nonspecific to confirm the disease. Tell: confirmation comes from a biopsy showing noncaseating granulomas.

Correct. Transbronchial biopsy of the lung or fine-needle node biopsy confirms sarcoidosis by showing noncaseating granulomas. Biopsy is essential whenever clinical and radiographic findings suggest the possibility of an alternative diagnosis such as lymphoma.

set2.q: After microscopic lung injury, what leads to pulmonary fibrosis rather than lung homeostasis?
opts: Both groups of stimuli, dust, fumes, cigarette smoke and autoimmune conditions on one side and drugs, infections, radiation and other diseases on the other, feed into the same microscopic injury. Tell: the fork toward fibrosis comes at wound healing, not at the stimulus.

The injury that starts the process is microscopic and separated spatially and temporally, not one large event. Whether it scars depends on how the wound heals. Tell: many small injuries over time, then intact versus aberrant healing decides the outcome.

Correct. Exogenous and endogenous stimuli cause microscopic lung injury, separated spatially and temporally. When wound healing is intact the lung returns to homeostasis; when it is aberrant, with genetic predisposition and autoimmune conditions acting on it, the result is pulmonary fibrosis.

Intact wound healing is the branch that returns the injured lung to homeostasis. Fibrosis follows the aberrant branch, which genetic predisposition and autoimmune conditions push toward. Tell: intact healing restores the lung, while aberrant healing scars it.

set2.q: How does cigarette smoking change the risks of asbestos exposure?
opts: It lowers the risk of mesothelioma
Smoking does not protect against mesothelioma: asbestos raises the risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma, especially in a smoker. Tell: smoking compounds asbestos risk rather than offsetting it.

Smoking increases the prevalence of radiographic pleural and parenchymal changes in asbestos-exposed patients, so the film is not unaffected. Tell: smoking worsens both the imaging changes and the cancer risk.
It speeds clearance of the fibers

Asbestos fibers invade lung tissue and cannot be removed, which is why treatment is supportive; smoking does nothing to clear them. Tell: the fibers stay for life, and smoking adds cancer risk on top of them.
It sharply raises lung cancer risk

Correct. In asbestos exposure, cigarette smoking increases the prevalence of radiographic pleural and parenchymal changes and markedly increases the incidence of lung carcinoma; the increased risk of lung cancer and mesothelioma applies especially to smokers.

set2.q: Which lung response do the connective tissue diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis produce?
opts: Correct. Connective tissue diseases (think autoimmune) such as systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis and Sjögren's syndrome produce an inflammatory and fibrotic lung response, the same group of response as asbestos, drugs and radiation.

A noncaseating granulomatous response is the sarcoidosis pattern, with T lymphocytes, macrophages and epithelioid cells organized into discrete granulomas. Tell: autoimmune connective tissue disease scars through inflammation and fibrosis rather than forming granulomas.
Interstitial lung disease is by definition not malignant, and the connective tissue group causes inflammation and fibrosis, not cancer. Tell: the autoimmune diseases inflame and scar the parenchyma.

Interstitial lung disease is not caused by an infectious etiology; connective tissue disease injures the lung through an autoimmune inflammatory and fibrotic response. Tell: think autoimmune, not infection, when lupus or rheumatoid arthritis involves the lung.

set2.q: A ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen of 80 mm Hg places acute respiratory distress syndrome in which severity class?
opts: Any ratio under 300 mm Hg meets the oxygenation criterion, so 80 is not outside it; it is the worst class. Tell: the scale runs mild, moderate, severe as the ratio falls, ending under 100 mm Hg.

Mild disease is a ratio of 200 to 300 mm Hg, far above 80, so mild badly underrates this degree of hypoxemia. Tell: the lower the ratio, the worse the class, and a ratio under 100 mm Hg is severe disease.

Moderate disease is a ratio of 100 to 200 mm Hg, and 80 lies below that band, so moderate underrates it. Tell: crossing under 100 mm Hg moves the class from moderate to severe, where salvage options are reserved.

Correct. A ratio of arterial oxygen pressure to fraction of inspired oxygen under 100 mm Hg is severe acute respiratory distress syndrome; 100 to 200 is moderate and 200 to 300 mild. Severe, refractory cases are where extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is reserved as salvage.

set2.q: When may the physical examination be normal in interstitial lung disease?
opts: Correct. Early in interstitial lung disease the examination may be normal. As the disease advances, small lung volumes, bibasilar dry rales or inspiratory crackles and distal clubbing appear, and right heart failure can develop with advanced disease.

Advanced disease is when the examination is most abnormal: small lung volumes, bibasilar inspiratory crackles, clubbing and even right heart failure. Tell: a normal examination belongs to early disease, not to established fibrosis.

Dyspnea at rest comes as the disease progresses, a later stage when crackles and small lung volumes are expected on examination. Tell: dyspnea at rest signals progression, while the normal examination comes early.

Right heart failure is itself an examination finding of advanced interstitial lung disease, so the examination is abnormal by then. Tell: right heart failure marks late disease, and a normal examination is an early-disease possibility.

set2.q: Which reticular pattern on chest radiograph is an early finding in interstitial lung disease?
opts: Coarse reticular opacities are cystic spaces, the coarsest grade on the scale, not the early finding. The early finding is the fine, ground-glass pattern. Tell: the grades run fine, medium and coarse, and the fine grade is the one labeled early.

Reticulonodular means reticular shadows overlapping with nodules, a pattern linked to sarcoidosis, not the early grade of the reticular scale. Tell: the early reticular finding is fine and ground-glass, without nodules.

Correct. Reticular, curvilinear opacities are graded fine, medium and coarse: the fine, ground-glass pattern is an early finding, medium honeycombing is a late finding, and coarse opacities are cystic spaces. Chest films also show low lung volumes with patchy opacities.

Honeycombing is the medium reticular pattern and a late finding, so it marks established fibrosis rather than early disease. Tell: early disease is the fine ground-glass pattern; honeycombing comes later, with advanced scarring.

set2.q: Which group makes up the most common interstitial lung diseases of known etiology?
opts: Idiopathic interstitial pneumonias are by definition of unknown cause, so they cannot be the most common known-etiology group. Tell: idiopathic means no cause is evident; the known-cause leaders are inhaled dusts, fumes and gases.

Infection is outside the definition of interstitial lung disease, which is not caused by an infectious etiology. The common known causes are occupational and environmental exposures. Tell: look for an inhaled exposure at work or in the environment, not for an infection.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. The most common interstitial lung diseases of known etiology come from occupational or environmental exposures: inorganic dusts, organic dusts, and fumes or gases. When a known cause is suspected, the exposure history at work and in the environment is where it is found.

Connective tissue diseases such as lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and systemic sclerosis cause an autoimmune inflammatory and fibrotic lung response, but they are not the group named as the most common known cause. Tell: the most common known cause is something inhaled at work or at home.

set2.q: Over what time course do most interstitial lung diseases present?
opts: An episodic presentation is less common and can be seen with hypersensitivity pneumonitis, where illness follows exposure to inhaled organic material. Tell: episodes point to an exposure-linked disease; most interstitial diseases progress steadily over months to years.

Correct. Most interstitial lung diseases present chronically, over months to years; idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, sarcoidosis, pneumoconiosis and connective tissue diseases present this way. Acute, subacute and episodic presentations are the less usual patterns.

Days to weeks is the acute presentation, which occurs with allergy, not the way most interstitial lung diseases begin. Tell: acute onset points to an allergic cause, while the usual course is chronic, over months to years.

Weeks to months is the subacute presentation; it may occur in any interstitial lung disease but is most common with sarcoidosis and drug-induced disease. Tell: subacute is the minority pattern of drugs and sarcoidosis; chronic is the usual one.

set2.q: In which setting should idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia be suspected?
opts: Serum antibodies to an inhaled agent

Antibodies to the agent in serum give a definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis, a known-cause disease from inhaled organic dust. Tell: an identified antigen excludes an idiopathic label, which is used when nothing explains the disease.
ruled out by a stated finding

Bilateral hilar adenopathy alone is stage I sarcoidosis on chest radiograph, the stage with the best prognosis, not the picture of a fibrosing interstitial pneumonia. Tell: enlarged nodes without parenchymal change mean sarcoidosis, not fibrosis.

Correct. Idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia should be suspected in a patient with unexplained interstitial lung disease; it is the most common diagnosis among patients with interstitial lung disease, and when no associated cause is evident the pattern is idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

Asbestos exposure is a known cause, an occupational disease with pleural plaques and ferruginous bodies. Idiopathic means no cause is evident. Tell: a named exposure points to a known-cause disease; the idiopathic diagnosis needs the disease to be unexplained.

set2.q: Which chest radiograph finding points to sarcoidosis or silicosis among the interstitial lung diseases?
opts: Correct. On chest radiography, hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy points to sarcoidosis or silicosis. Sarcoidosis shows symmetric bilateral hilar and right paratracheal adenopathy, and silicosis can calcify the periphery of the hilar nodes in an eggshell pattern.

Pleural plaques are the most common chest radiograph finding in asbestosis, seen with linear streaking at the bases. They do not point to sarcoidosis or silicosis. Tell: pleural plaques mean asbestos; enlarged hilar nodes mean sarcoidosis or silicosis.

A normal heart size with air bronchograms and bilateral infiltrates that become confluent is the imaging of acute respiratory distress syndrome, not of a chronic granulomatous or dust disease. Tell: acute confluent infiltrates mean distress syndrome; enlarged nodes mean sarcoidosis or silicosis.

Diffuse patchy fibrosis with pleural-based honeycombing is the computed tomography picture of idiopathic fibrosing interstitial pneumonia, a late fibrotic finding. Tell: honeycombing means established fibrosis, while enlarged hilar and mediastinal nodes point to sarcoidosis or silicosis.

set2.q: Which test helps exclude cardiogenic pulmonary edema when acute respiratory distress syndrome is suspected?
opts: Routine pulmonary artery catheters offer no clinical benefit in acute respiratory distress syndrome and are to be avoided. Tell: cardiac function is assessed with echocardiography, the noninvasive test named for excluding cardiogenic edema.

Bronchoalveolar lavage samples the airspaces, for example the thick, milky effluent of silicosis; it does not assess cardiac function. Tell: excluding a cardiac cause of edema needs a look at the heart, which echocardiography provides.

Pulmonary function testing shows the restrictive pattern of interstitial lung disease; it does not evaluate the heart. Tell: to exclude hydrostatic cardiogenic edema, assess cardiac function by echocardiography.

Correct. Echocardiographic assessment evaluates cardiac function to exclude hydrostatic cardiogenic pulmonary edema, the main differential. Supporting this, the heart size is normal in acute respiratory distress syndrome, with minimal or absent pleural effusions.

set2.q: Which medication is used for sarcoidosis that is intolerant of or refractory to corticosteroids?
opts: Correct. Immunosuppressive medications, most commonly methotrexate, azathioprine or infliximab, are used in patients with sarcoidosis who are intolerant of corticosteroids or who have corticosteroid-refractory disease. About 90% of cases otherwise respond to corticosteroids.

Amiodarone is a treatment-related cause of interstitial lung disease and of drug-induced pulmonary toxicity, not a sarcoidosis therapy. Tell: amiodarone injures the lung, while the steroid-sparing agents are methotrexate, azathioprine and infliximab.

Nitrofurantoin is in the treatment-related box of interstitial lung disease causes and causes drug-induced pulmonary toxicity, so it would add lung injury rather than control sarcoidosis. Tell: it is a cause of lung disease, not an immunosuppressant.

Bronchodilators appear as supportive treatment in hypersensitivity pneumonitis, beside oxygen and pain medication; they do not suppress granulomatous inflammation. Tell: steroid-refractory sarcoidosis needs an immunosuppressant such as methotrexate, azathioprine or infliximab.

set2.q: Which finding gives a definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis?
opts: Chest radiograph and computed tomography show little change acutely, with fibrotic changes only in subacute and chronic disease, so a normal-looking film cannot define the diagnosis. Tell: imaging lags; antibodies to the agent confirm.

Correct. Antibodies to the agent in serum give a definitive diagnosis of hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Supporting findings include an elevated white blood cell count with a left shift, hypoxia and restrictive pulmonary function, and lung biopsy may be indicated in subacute or chronic disease.
White cell count with left shift

An elevated white blood cell count with a left shift supports the diagnosis but does not identify the antigen, so it is not definitive. Tell: inflammation markers support; antibodies to the specific agent define.

Restrictive dysfunction is common to many interstitial lung diseases, from idiopathic fibrosis to asbestosis, so it cannot single out hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Tell: restriction is shared, while antibodies to the agent are specific.

set2.q: What do macrophages, lymphocytes, monocytes and neutrophils accumulating in the alveolar walls first produce?
opts: Correct. In the pathophysiology of fibrosis, macrophages, lymphocytes, monocytes and neutrophils accumulate in the alveolar walls and alveolitis occurs. Alveolitis then leads to fibroblast production, and the collagen those fibroblasts produce causes the fibrosis.

Collagen comes later in the sequence: alveolitis leads to fibroblast production, and the fibroblasts make the collagen that causes fibrosis. Tell: the inflammatory cells first cause alveolitis; collagen is the end product, two steps further on.

Honeycombing is the medium reticular pattern on imaging, a late finding once fibrosis is established, not the first result of inflammatory cells gathering in the alveolar walls. Tell: honeycombing is late imaging; alveolitis is the first tissue step.

Granulomas belong to the other response group: T lymphocytes, macrophages and epithelioid cells organized into discrete structures in the parenchyma. The fibrotic sequence starts with alveolitis instead. Tell: discrete organized lesions mean granulomatous; inflamed alveolar walls mean alveolitis.
